name: Solid motor
flight: Lifts 600 kg. Steers in fixed pulses.
fact: Solid boosters give huge thrust but cannot be throttled or shut down once lit. The Shuttle and SLS pair them with liquid engines for control.

name: Chemical engine
fact: The RL10 has flown since the 1960s because it restarts and throttles cleanly, but every burn spends propellant that had to be launched too.

name: Ion drive
fact: Dawn's ion engines pushed about as hard as a sheet of paper weighs, but ran for years on very little xenon and visited two worlds.

name: Small solar array
surface: Slow suit recharge, weak at Mars
fact: InSight ran on two small solar arrays. Mars dust slowly covered them, and the mission ended in 2022 when power ran out.

name: Large solar array
flight: Plenty of power, bigger debris target.
fact: Juno flies three 9 m solar wings to make about 500 W at Jupiter, where sunlight is 25 times weaker than at Earth. Big arrays are big targets.

name: Radioisotope generator
fact: Curiosity and Perseverance carry an MMRTG, so dust storms and night do not stop them. Its waste heat has to be managed all the time.

name: Low-gain antenna
fact: Rovers keep a low-gain antenna because it needs no pointing, but it sends only a trickle. Most science goes home through an orbiter's bigger dish.

name: High-gain dish
fact: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter carries a 3 m dish so its cameras' data can get home. A strong instrument needs a link that can keep up.

name: Laser terminal
real: Deep Space Optical Comms on Psyche
fact: The Deep Space Optical Communications demo on Psyche sent data by laser far faster than radio, but the beam has to be pointed with extreme precision.

name: Camera
fact: HiRISE takes the sharpest pictures of Mars from orbit. One image can be gigabytes, so the camera is only as useful as the link that sends it home.

name: Spectrometer
fact: SuperCam fires a laser at rocks from up to 7 m away and reads the light to learn what they are made of. Its detectors have to be kept cool to work.

name: Radar sounder
fact: SHARAD sees layers of ice and rock below the Martian surface, but it needs a lot of power and a spacecraft built around it.

name: Salvage motor
fact: Real missions pick the engine first, because it decides how much everything else is allowed to weigh.

name: Salvage battery
fact: Real missions size the power system with margin. Running a spacecraft at its power limit leaves nothing for a bad day.

name: Salvage antenna
fact: Every mission plans how its data gets home before launch. NASA's Deep Space Network is booked years ahead, and a weak antenna wastes every minute of it.

name: Salvage camera
fact: Instruments are chosen to answer one science question. A spare camera that was never meant for the job brings back data nobody planned for.
